events.title: First ARPANET Message
events.blurb: A graduate student at a California university tried to log in remotely to a computer at a research institute 560 kilometres north. He typed "L," then "O," then tried to type "G" — and the receiving computer crashed. The first ever message transmitted between two computers on what would grow into the global network was thus the two-letter sequence "lo."
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1969 — UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute. The student was Charley Kline. ARPANET was funded by the Pentagon to enable communication after a nuclear strike. The network went from 4 nodes to 37 in three years.

events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: Napster Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Northeastern University student released a peer-to-peer file-sharing program that let any user share their digitized music collection with any other user, anywhere in the world. Within 18 months, 80 million registered users were trading tens of millions of MP3 files a day. The recording industry sued; one rock band's lead drummer famously delivered a list of his fans using the service to Napster's offices in person.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1999 — Shawn Fanning. The suing drummer was Lars Ulrich of Metallica. Napster was shut down by a 2001 court ruling; the brand was later bought, sold, and reused several times, most recently by Algorand.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: Snowden Leaks Begin
events.blurb: Two newspapers published articles based on documents leaked by a 29-year-old former NSA contractor, revealing that the U.S. government had been conducting bulk collection of American phone records from a major telecommunications company under a secret court order. The revelations continued for years; the leaker fled to Hong Kong and, after attempting to transit to Ecuador, spent years stranded in the transit zone of a Moscow airport.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 2013 — Edward Snowden, via Glenn Greenwald at The Guardian and Barton Gellman at The Washington Post. Snowden received Russian citizenship in September 2022. Remains wanted on espionage charges in the U.S.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Hillary and Tenzing Summit Everest
events.blurb: A 33-year-old New Zealand beekeeper and a 39-year-old Nepalese sherpa, the final two-man summit party of a British Himalayan expedition, stepped onto the top of the world's highest mountain at 11:30 AM local time after a four-hour climb from their high camp. They spent fifteen minutes at the top, took photographs, and buried a few mementos in the snow. News reached London on the morning of the queen's coronation four days later.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1953 — Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, British expedition under John Hunt. They never conclusively settled which of them stepped onto the summit first; both said it didn't matter. The news coincided with Queen Elizabeth II's coronation, making it front-page across the Commonwealth.

events.title: Secretariat Wins the Triple Crown
events.blurb: A three-year-old chestnut colt won the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in a world-record time of 2 minutes 24 seconds, becoming the first Triple Crown winner in 25 years. His margin of victory and track record remain unmatched; television viewers watching the broadcast described the race as looking like a different event from the others.

events.title: Cubs Win World Series
events.blurb: The Chicago Cubs won their first World Series championship in 108 years, defeating the Cleveland Indians in a 10-inning seventh game interrupted by a rain delay. The Cubs' championship drought — dating back to 1908 — was the longest in American professional sports. Their 1945 loss had been attributed by fans to the "Curse of the Billy Goat," thrown at the owner of a neighbourhood tavern who had been asked to remove his pet goat from a World Series game.
events.revealBlurb: November 2-3, 2016 — Cubs 8, Indians 7 in 10 innings at Progressive Field, Cleveland. The game ended at 12:47 AM local time on November 3. Cubs manager Joe Maddon, third baseman Kris Bryant, and first baseman Anthony Rizzo led the championship team. Chicago celebrated with a victory parade of 5 million people.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Invented
events.blurb: A Lancashire weaver, semi-literate and working out of his home, built a hand-cranked multi-spindle spinning frame that let one operator spin eight threads simultaneously rather than one. Later versions spun up to 120 spindles at once. Other weavers' wives in the district, seeing their cottage-industry spinning work disappearing, broke into his house and smashed his prototypes. He patented the invention six years later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1764 — James Hargreaves in Blackburn, England. Patented 1770. The name "Jenny" is probably derived from "gin," a contemporary term for a mechanical engine — not, contrary to popular story, after his daughter. Hargreaves died in poverty in 1778.

events.title: Great Reform Act
events.blurb: A long-delayed parliamentary reform bill received royal assent in Britain after two years of political crisis that nearly toppled the government. The act abolished 56 "rotten boroughs" — constituencies with almost no voters but a parliamentary seat still in the pocket of a local landowner — redistributed seats to industrial cities that had grown dramatically since the previous redistricting in 1429, and raised the adult male electorate from about 400,000 to 650,000.
events.revealBlurb: June 7, 1832 — royal assent by William IV, after the government threatened to flood the House of Lords with new peers to force passage. It was the first of a sequence of 19th-century reform acts; universal male suffrage in Britain was not achieved until 1918, and women over 30 the same year.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: "We Shall Fight" Speech
events.blurb: A prime minister who had been in office barely a month stood in a parliamentary chamber and delivered a report on a catastrophic military retreat, then pivoted to an uncompromising catalogue of every terrain — beaches, landing grounds, fields, streets, hills — across which his country would resist, closing with a flat refusal to ever surrender.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1940 — Churchill's "We Shall Fight on the Beaches" speech to the House of Commons. He reportedly muttered to a colleague immediately after: "And we'll fight them with the butt ends of broken beer bottles because that's bloody well all we've got." The line never made the official record.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: D-Day Landings
events.blurb: 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five code-named beaches along an 80-kilometre stretch of Normandy coast, supported by 11,000 aircraft sorties and 7,000 naval vessels. A massive deception operation convinced enemy commanders the real target was 300 kilometres further east.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 1944 — Operation Overlord. Eisenhower carried a note in his pocket taking full blame if it failed. The "Mulberry" artificial harbours, towed across the Channel in pieces, unloaded two million tons of supplies in the months that followed. The first soldier ashore on Sword Beach was a British piper playing "Blue Bonnets Over the Border."

events.title: Fall of Monte Cassino
events.blurb: After four separate offensives spanning five months, Polish troops raised their flag over the ruins of a hilltop monastery that had been reduced to rubble by an Allied bombing raid — finally cracking a mountain defensive line that had blocked the Allied advance up a peninsula for half a year and cost over 43,000 casualties across all the assaulting armies.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1944. Polish Corps commander General Anders had promised his men they would fight for Poland in the west since the Soviet Union had taken the east. Over 900 Polish soldiers died in the final assault. The monastery's Benedictine monks had evacuated its art treasures months earlier; the abbey itself was empty during the famous Allied bombing of February 15.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Colombian journalist living in Mexico City published a novel tracing seven generations of the Buendía family in the imaginary Caribbean town of Macondo, blending precise historical detail with flying carpets, ghosts, and a character who slowly levitates. The first printing of 8,000 copies sold out in a week. The book invented "magical realism" as a recognized literary mode and cemented its author as the dominant figure in Latin American letters.
events.revealBlurb: June 5, 1967 — Gabriel García Márquez ("Gabo"). He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. He wrote the book in eighteen months while his wife pawned their possessions to pay the grocer. It has sold over 50 million copies.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Death of Alexander the Great
events.blurb: A Macedonian king who had conquered territory from Greece to northwest India died after a two-week fever in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in Babylon, aged 32. His generals immediately divided his empire into competing successor kingdoms, triggering a half-century of wars called the Wars of the Diadochi.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.blurb: A Roman general's army of 70,000 legionaries, closing the siege of a rebellious Judean capital after a four-year Jewish revolt, breached the walls and burned the city's Second Temple on the anniversary of the first Temple's destruction 656 years earlier. The Temple was never rebuilt; a Western retaining wall remains the holiest site in Judaism. Roman troops hauled the Temple menorah and other sacred vessels to Rome, where a victory arch depicting the procession still stands.
events.revealBlurb: 70 CE — the siege was commanded by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian. The Arch of Titus, completed c. 81 CE, still stands at the east end of the Roman Forum. The Western Wall is the most significant surviving fragment; Orthodox Jews mourn the Temple's destruction each year on Tisha B'Av.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.blurb: A Roman general of Germanic birth led a coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians, and Alans against a massive Hunnic invasion of Gaul under their formidable king. The battle — one of the largest ever fought in antiquity — ended in an indecisive but bloody Roman-allied victory that stopped the Huns' westward expansion. The Hunnic king would die suddenly two years later on his wedding night from a burst blood vessel; his empire collapsed within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: 451 CE — Flavius Aetius (Roman) and Theodoric I (Visigoth) vs. Attila the Hun. Theodoric was killed in the battle. Attila's death in 453, on his wedding night to a Germanic princess named Ildico, was probably from an esophageal hemorrhage. His sons squabbled; the Hunnic Empire dissolved.

events.title: CNN Launches
events.blurb: A 24-hour cable news network began broadcasting from a converted country-club headquarters in a southeastern U.S. city, defying widespread industry skepticism that there was enough daily news to fill a full day of programming. The network's first broadcast began with its founder and his wife standing in front of an American flag. Its approach — continuous live coverage, rolling updates, no fixed broadcast schedule — eventually reshaped how all news was delivered.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1980 — Ted Turner's Cable News Network, Atlanta. The Gulf War coverage in 1991, broadcast live from Baghdad as bombs fell, established CNN's dominance. Turner had filmed a doomsday video, intended to play only at the literal end of the world, saying farewell to viewers.

events.title: "Who Shot J.R.?" Revealed
events.blurb: An estimated 83 million American viewers — 76 percent of all active television sets at the time — tuned in to a prime-time U.S. soap opera to learn who had fired the cliffhanger-ending shot that had kept the nation guessing for eight months. At the time it was the most-watched single program in television history. Souvenir T-shirts, novelty songs, and betting pools had all sprouted during the summer hiatus between seasons.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1980 — Dallas, episode "Who Done It." The shooter was Kristin Shepard, played by Mary Crosby. J.R. Ewing survived. The "Who Shot J.R.?" plot is considered a pioneer of the season-ending cliffhanger in prime-time television.

events.title: Ghostbusters Released
events.blurb: A comedy directed by and starring several members of a Saturday Night Live cast followed a team of parapsychology PhDs turned paranormal exterminators in New York City. The film grossed $282 million on a $30 million budget and became the highest-grossing comedy to that point. Its theme song, written under deadline pressure, sat at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. A marshmallow man the size of a skyscraper became the film's most memorable villain.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1984 — Ivan Reitman directing Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Harold Ramis, and Ernie Hudson. Theme song by Ray Parker Jr. The marshmallow costume, worn by actor William Atherton, weighed 45 kg and caused heat exhaustion.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.

events.title: Prabhat Film Company Founded
events.blurb: Five filmmakers and one jeweller-financier pooled ₹15,000 in a Kolhapur courtyard and established a studio whose name meant "Dawn" — it would go on to produce landmark Marathi and Hindi films through the 1930s, win the first Venice Film Festival prize awarded to an Asian film, and whose abandoned compound would later house the country's national film school.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1929 — founded by V. Shantaram and associates. Their 1936 film Sant Tukaram won a Venice award. When the studio folded in 1953, its Pune premises became the site of the Film and Television Institute of India.

events.title: Anand Released
events.blurb: A terminally ill man facing lymphosarcoma of the intestine spends his remaining months arguing that life is worth celebrating — while his doctor-friend records him in a notebook — in a film whose two leads delivered career-defining performances on opposite emotional registers. Its final line, spoken after death, became among the most quoted in Hindi cinema.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1971 — directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee, dialogues by Gulzar. Rajesh Khanna was at the absolute peak of his popularity; Amitabh Bachchan was still a supporting player. The film reportedly made Amitabh Bachchan weep on set during the final sequence — which Mukherjee kept in the film.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: Lagaan Nominated for Academy Award
events.blurb: A four-hour cricket epic set under British colonial rule — filmed largely in a Gujarat village with a cast of thousands, shot in Hindi with English-speaking British actors, and assembled into a musical — was selected as India's submission to the Academy Awards and became only the third Indian film in history to receive a Best Foreign Language Film nomination.
events.revealBlurb: Released June 15, 2001; Oscar nomination announced February 2002. Aamir Khan both produced and starred. The film was shot in the searing Bhuj heat over 75 days. Its cricket finale runs 20 minutes and was edited like a sporting thriller — at the time considered unbankably risky for a Bollywood audience.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: Pythagorean Theorem Proven in Greek School
events.blurb: Greek mathematicians of the Pythagorean school produced the first known formal proof that in any right-angled triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two — a relationship that had been known empirically by Babylonian and Egyptian surveyors for over a thousand years, but never demonstrated to follow necessarily from first principles.
events.revealBlurb: c. 530 BCE — the theorem was known to Babylonian scribes by 1900 BCE, long before Pythagoras was born. What his school contributed was the idea of proving it. There are over 370 known distinct proofs; one appears in Euclid's Elements, another was submitted by a sitting U.S. President (James Garfield) to a mathematics journal in 1876.

events.title: Copernican Heliocentric Model Published
events.blurb: A six-volume astronomical treatise placed the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the universe, arguing that Earth was just one of several planets orbiting the Sun and that Earth's own daily rotation explained the apparent motion of the stars. The author received the first printed copy on the day he died.
events.revealBlurb: 1543 — Copernicus sat on the manuscript for years, fearing ridicule. A colleague secretly arranged its publication; legend holds the author held the final printed pages on his deathbed. The Church placed the book on its Index of Forbidden Books 73 years after publication — once it actually started to threaten orthodoxy.

events.title: Photoelectric Effect Explained
events.blurb: A paper explained why shining light on a metal surface ejects electrons only when the light exceeds a threshold frequency — never for very bright low-frequency light — by proposing that light itself travels in discrete energy packets rather than continuous waves. The finding resolved a long-standing paradox and extended the quantum idea from heat radiation to light, fundamentally changing the understanding of what light is.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1905 — this was the paper that explicitly won Einstein the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not relativity. When the Nobel Committee finally awarded it (sixteen years late), they cited this discovery specifically. Einstein reportedly joked that the committee must have found relativity too controversial.

events.title: Continental Drift Hypothesis Presented
events.blurb: A German meteorologist proposed that Earth's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent that had since broken apart and drifted slowly across the ocean floor, citing the geometric fit of coastlines, matching fossil records on opposite sides of the Atlantic, and ancient glacial scour marks in tropical regions. The geological community's response was immediate and largely hostile.
events.revealBlurb: January 6, 1912 — Alfred Wegener's hypothesis was mocked at a major American geological meeting in 1926, where a speaker suggested geologists should "be instantly prepared to disregard" it. Wegener died on a Greenland expedition in 1930. The mechanism he was missing — seafloor spreading — was found by Harry Hess in the 1960s.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: Marie Curie Wins Nobel Prize
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Polish-born physicist working in a converted shed in a French capital became the first woman to win the world's most prestigious scientific prize, sharing a physics award with her husband and a French colleague for their research into radioactivity. She would win it a second time, alone, in chemistry eight years later. Her notebooks are still radioactive, stored in lead-lined boxes and read only in protective clothing.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1903 — shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She later became the first person, of any gender, to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her daughter Irène won a Nobel in chemistry too.

events.title: UK Women Get the Vote
events.blurb: A British parliament, persuaded partly by the contribution of women to the wartime labour force, enfranchised women householders and university graduates aged 30 and over — extending the franchise to about 8.5 million new voters. Complete parity with men would take another decade. One of its first fruits was the election, shortly after, of a woman to the Commons, who declined to take her seat.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1918 — Representation of the People Act. The non-taking-her-seat member was Constance Markievicz, elected for Sinn Féin in Dublin; she refused to swear allegiance to the Crown. Women 21-29 got the vote in 1928.

events.title: Equal Pay Act Signed
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed legislation making it unlawful for employers to pay women less than men for equal work on jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility. The law had been introduced 18 years earlier and passed only after being narrowed so far that it exempted executive, administrative, and professional employees — and explicitly did not cover many of the sex-segregated job categories where the pay gap was worst.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1963 — John F. Kennedy. It amended the Fair Labor Standards Act. The wage gap between full-time working men and women has narrowed from 60 cents on the dollar in 1963 to roughly 82 cents today — not yet zero, and progress stalled for most of the 2010s.

events.title: Valentina Tereshkova in Space
events.blurb: A 26-year-old textile-factory worker and amateur parachutist from a provincial Russian town orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days aboard a Vostok capsule, becoming the first woman in space. She was two decades ahead of the next woman cosmonaut. Western intelligence had no idea the Soviet Union had even trained female cosmonauts. The mission, like all Soviet space missions, was announced only after the launch.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Her call sign was "Chaika" (Seagull). Over half a century later, aged 85, Tereshkova remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission. The next Soviet woman cosmonaut flew 19 years later.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Psycho Released
events.blurb: A British-American director released a black-and-white thriller for a third of his usual budget, using his television crew, that broke every Hollywood rule: its marketed star was killed in the shower 45 minutes in, the real story shifted to a different protagonist, and theatrical exhibitors were barred from letting latecomers enter. The 45-second shower sequence, involving 77 camera setups in a week of filming, became the most analyzed passage in thriller cinema.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1960 — Alfred Hitchcock, starring Janet Leigh and Anthony Perkins. Hitchcock personally bought up copies of the Robert Bloch novel to limit spoilers. The shower-stabbing sound was a knife thrust into a casaba melon.

events.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial Released
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American director released a 115-minute family film about a stranded alien befriended by a suburban boy who helps him contact his home planet. The director had developed the story as a way of processing his parents' divorce and his imaginary childhood companion. The film topped the box office for 16 weeks, displaced Star Wars as the highest-grossing film of all time, and moved children to tears for decades.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1982 — Steven Spielberg. Composer John Williams won the Oscar for his score; Spielberg himself didn't. The flying-bicycle silhouette against the moon became the logo of Amblin Entertainment, his production company.

events.title: 15th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: A constitutional amendment prohibiting the denial of voting rights "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude" was ratified, giving Black men the theoretical right to vote. Within three decades, poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and organized terror had effectively erased Black voting across the former Confederacy.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1870. It took the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — 95 years later — to make the amendment's promise practical. Black women were excluded not by race but by sex until the 19th Amendment in 1920.

events.title: Jackie Robinson Breaks Color Barrier
events.blurb: A 28-year-old second baseman took the field at a Brooklyn ballpark and became the first African-American to play in modern Major League Baseball, breaking a 63-year color line enforced by gentlemen's agreement rather than written rule. He went hitless in his debut but reached base on an error and scored the winning run.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1947 — Ebbets Field, Brooklyn Dodgers. Team president Branch Rickey had signed him with the understanding he would absorb abuse without retaliation for two years. Robinson's number 42 was retired across every MLB team in 1997, the only such universal retirement in sports.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: Medgar Evers Assassinated
events.blurb: The NAACP's field secretary in a Southern state was shot in the back in his own driveway as he returned home at 12:30 AM from a meeting, carrying T-shirts that read "Jim Crow Must Go." He died in front of his wife and three children. His killer, a Ku Klux Klan member, was tried twice; both trials ended in hung juries with all-white panels. He walked free for 31 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1963 — Jackson, Mississippi. His killer, Byron De La Beckwith, was finally convicted in 1994 after new witnesses came forward. Medgar's widow Myrlie Evers-Williams spent decades pursuing the case; she later chaired the NAACP.

events.title: Loving v. Virginia
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously struck down the laws of sixteen states prohibiting interracial marriage, after a Virginia couple — a white construction worker and his Black and Native American wife — had been awakened in their bed, arrested, and sentenced to a year in jail for being married. The Court called the bans "measures designed to maintain White Supremacy."
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1967 — Richard and Mildred Loving. They had been legally married in Washington D.C. and returned home to Virginia. Their surname's poetic appropriateness is real, not invented. June 12 is now informally "Loving Day."

events.title: 18th Amendment: Prohibition Ratified
events.blurb: Nebraska became the 36th state to ratify the 18th Amendment, providing the three-fourths supermajority needed to ban the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors in the United States. The amendment went into effect one year later, launching a 13-year experiment in moral legislation that spawned organized crime, enriched bootleggers, and ended with the 21st Amendment's repeal.
events.revealBlurb: January 16, 1919 — ratified in less than 11 months, the fastest major amendment in history to that point. Al Capone made an estimated $60 million a year ($1.1 billion today) during Prohibition.

events.title: Taft-Hartley Act Becomes Law
events.blurb: The Republican-controlled 80th Congress overrode President Harry Truman's veto, enacting the Labor-Management Relations Act — known as Taft-Hartley — which restricted union activities, banned secondary boycotts and solidarity strikes, permitted states to pass right-to-work laws, and required union officers to swear they were not Communists. The law fundamentally reshaped the relationship between organized labor and the federal government.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1947 — Washington, D.C. Truman called it a "slave labor bill" in his veto message, though he later used its provisions himself to break the 1952 steel strike. Union membership peaked at about 35% of the workforce in the late 1940s; by 2024 it had fallen to roughly 10%.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Reagan: "Tear Down This Wall"
events.blurb: Standing 100 yards from the concrete barrier dividing East and West Berlin that afternoon, President Ronald Reagan delivered a speech at the Brandenburg Gate in which he directly challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" His own State Department and National Security Council had urged him to remove the line as counterproductively provocative; Reagan insisted on keeping it.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin. At the time, the speech received relatively little media coverage and was dismissed as Cold War posturing by Soviet state media. Two years, four months, and 27 days later, the wall fell.

events.title: September 11 Terrorist Attacks
events.blurb: That morning, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers commandeered four commercial aircraft and flew two into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and a fourth — whose passengers revolted and forced the plane down — into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the United States' longest wars, a sweeping reorganization of domestic security, and a generation of political consequence.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — New York, Virginia, Pennsylvania. The North Tower stood 102 minutes after impact; the South Tower collapsed first, 56 minutes after being hit, because the plane struck lower floors. The 9/11 Commission found no credible evidence of state sponsorship by any foreign government.

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith
events.blurb: A Roman painter in her mid-twenties completed a large oil on canvas of a biblical heroine and her maidservant beheading an Assyrian general — a scene painted by many male artists before her, but never this physically, with two women straining against the weight of the act and blood spraying across the sheets. The painter had been raped and then tortured with thumbscrews during the trial of her rapist seven years earlier; the subject matter was not accidental.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1620 — Artemisia Gentileschi. Now in Naples' Museo di Capodimonte. An earlier version she painted between 1611 and 1613 hangs in Florence's Uffizi. Gentileschi became the first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia delle Arti del Disegno.

events.title: Van Gogh Paints The Starry Night
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter, voluntarily committed to a mental asylum in a Provençal town, painted from memory — and through the bars of his east-facing window — a night sky filled with swirling nebulae and stars dozens of times their actual size, above a village with an exaggeratedly prominent church steeple. He considered the painting a failure. It is now among the most recognized images in Western art.
events.revealBlurb: June 1889 — Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The village in the picture does not match the actual view. The Museum of Modern Art in New York has owned it since 1941. Recent research suggests the sky's swirls resemble actual fluid turbulence.

events.title: Dalí's Persistence of Memory
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Spanish surrealist painted a small oil on canvas — only 24 by 33 cm — showing four pocket watches, one covered in ants, draped limply over a tree branch, a bier, and a distorted horse-headed figure in a landscape of Catalan coast. He said the idea came from contemplating a runny camembert cheese. The ants, the soft watches, and the empty landscape have become visual shorthand for dreamlike unreality.
events.revealBlurb: 1931 — Salvador Dalí. Now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Dalí painted a second version, "The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory," 23 years later. He is said to have visualized in reverse: imagining the picture whole and then painting what he saw.

events.title: Pollock's Drip Paintings
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American painter, working in a converted barn studio on Long Island, laid large unstretched canvases on the floor and moved around their edges pouring and flinging paint from sticks and hardened brushes. The resulting "drip paintings" rejected representational composition entirely in favour of overall visual rhythm. A 1949 Life magazine spread asked: "Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?" and made him instantly famous and nearly famously alcoholic.
events.revealBlurb: 1947 — Jackson Pollock began the drip technique in Springs, NY. He died in a car crash driving drunk on August 11, 1956, aged 44. His "No. 5, 1948" sold privately in 2006 for $140 million, briefly the highest price ever paid for a painting.

events.title: Sack of Lindisfarne
events.blurb: A band of Scandinavian raiders beached their longships on the tidal island home of an isolated monastery off the northeast coast of England, slaughtered the monks, and plundered the gold and silver from the gilded shrines. The attack shocked Christian Europe, which had not imagined its remote religious outposts were vulnerable. It marks the conventional beginning of the Viking Age.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 793 — the monks had left their community undefended on the assumption that the sea was a barrier rather than a road. Alcuin, one of Charlemagne's advisers, wrote: "Never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have suffered from this pagan race."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Hundred Years' War Begins
events.blurb: An English king, claiming the French throne through his mother on the extinction of the main French royal line, formally renounced his homage for his continental territories and declared himself the rightful king of France. The resulting dynastic war would last 116 years across five generations, introduce the longbow as a battlefield weapon, and eventually produce the nation-states of France and England.
events.revealBlurb: 1337 — Edward III vs. Philip VI. The conflict ran in spasms with long truces, and is named "Hundred Years" only in retrospect. Joan of Arc arrived in its fifth generation; gunpowder arrived in its fourth.

events.title: First Woman in Space
events.blurb: Valentina Tereshkova, a 26-year-old former textile factory worker and amateur parachutist with no pilot training, launched aboard Vostok 6 and orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days — more total time in space than all US astronauts who had flown to that date combined. She performed observations and photographed aerosol layers in Earth's atmosphere before parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Tereshkova selected herself from 400 applicants by writing a letter directly to the Soviet Space Program. She reportedly got motion sick and did not conduct some planned manual maneuvers, a fact kept classified for years. No woman flew in space again for 19 years. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: First Mars Close-Up Flyby
events.blurb: Mariner 4 flew within 9,846 km of Mars and transmitted 21 photographs covering about 1% of the planet's surface — the first close-range images of another planet. The images revealed a cratered, Moon-like landscape and showed Mars had a much thinner atmosphere than expected, with a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars, dashing hopes of a habitable world.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4. The images took four days to receive and were so eagerly anticipated that JPL technicians printed the first strips of data by hand onto paper using artist's pastels, coloring by number before the computer could process the file. The result was a blurry colored rectangle they pinned to a bulletin board.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: First Commercial Crewed Orbital Launch
events.blurb: SpaceX Crew Dragon Endeavour launched two NASA astronauts to the International Space Station, marking the first crewed orbital launch from American soil since the Space Shuttle's retirement nine years earlier and the first time a commercially built and operated vehicle carried NASA astronauts to orbit. The spacecraft docked with the ISS approximately 19 hours after liftoff.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 2020 — Demo-2. The launch was originally scrubbed three days earlier at T-17 minutes due to a storm. Astronaut Doug Hurley — who had piloted the final Shuttle mission in 2011 — flew his second "last American launch from US soil" in nine years, except this time it wasn't the last. The touchscreen controls in the Dragon capsule replaced 800+ switches.

events.title: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
events.blurb: Tradition holds that a Babylonian king built a tiered rooftop garden at his palace for his wife, homesick for the mountainous landscape of her native Media. The structure — described by Greek writers as having stone terraces planted with trees and shrubs irrigated by an elaborate water-lifting machine — was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. No archaeological evidence of them has ever been identified at Babylon, leading some scholars to believe they existed instead at Nineveh under a different king.
events.revealBlurb: c. 600 BCE — traditionally attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II. A leading alternative theory attributes them to Sennacherib at Nineveh, a century earlier. Of the Seven Wonders, only the Pyramids survive and the Hanging Gardens are the one whose very existence is still in question.

events.title: Great Wall of China Begun
events.blurb: The first emperor of a unified Chinese state, having conquered the six rival warring kingdoms, ordered existing regional defensive walls in the north linked into a continuous frontier fortification against nomadic incursions. A conscripted army of 300,000 labourers worked for years; many died on the project and were, according to tradition, buried in its foundations. The Ming-dynasty wall, which is what most modern visitors see, was rebuilt over a millennium later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 220 BCE — Qin Shi Huang. The visible stone-and-brick wall is largely Ming-dynasty (1368-1644), built with much better materials. The Qin wall was mostly earthen and only fragments survive. Total length, across all versions, has been measured at 21,196 km.

events.title: Colosseum Inaugurated
events.blurb: A Roman emperor inaugurated a 50,000-capacity elliptical amphitheatre in the capital with 100 consecutive days of gladiatorial games, executions, and staged hunts that killed 9,000 animals. The structure was four stories tall, constructed in travertine and concrete, with a retractable canvas awning (velarium) to shade the spectators. Its name comes from the colossal statue of an earlier emperor that stood nearby. Three quarters of the building still stands today.
events.revealBlurb: 80 CE — inaugurated by Emperor Titus, son of Vespasian who had started construction eight years earlier. The colossal statue in question was of Nero, which Vespasian had rededicated as the sun god. Most of the travertine facing was stripped in medieval times for Renaissance building projects.

events.title: Notre-Dame de Paris Completed
events.blurb: The main fabric of a Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine at the heart of the French capital was finished after 182 years of construction. Its twin western towers, flying buttresses, three great rose windows, and vast nave became the template for French Gothic architecture. It survived the Wars of Religion, the French Revolution (when it was briefly rededicated to a "Cult of Reason"), Haussmann's 19th-century restorations, and two world wars — before a fire in 2019 collapsed its 19th-century spire and much of its roof.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1345 — Notre-Dame cathedral, Paris. Construction began in 1163. The 19th-century restoration was led by Eugène Viollet-le-Duc. The 2019 fire's cause was never conclusively determined; reconstruction was completed in December 2024.

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown
events.blurb: A British army of 8,000 men under a peer of the realm, trapped on a Virginia peninsula by a combined Franco-American land force and blocked from the Chesapeake by a French fleet, surrendered after a three-week siege. The British commander, reportedly feigning illness, sent a deputy to the surrender ceremony; his band played a tune called "The World Turned Upside Down." The war dragged on in minor engagements for two more years but the outcome was no longer in doubt.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 1781 — Lord Cornwallis surrenders to General George Washington and Comte de Rochambeau at Yorktown, Virginia. The French navy's blockade, commanded by Admiral de Grasse, decided the siege. Formal peace negotiations began within months.

events.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.blurb: The French National Constituent Assembly, meeting in a recently converted royal indoor tennis court, adopted a 17-article statement of universal rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of speech and religion. It did not grant women the vote or abolish slavery; revolutionaries would debate those extensions for years. It was still the most sweeping such declaration any European state had ever adopted.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1789 — a central drafter was the Marquis de Lafayette, the American Revolution veteran. The declaration was explicitly modeled on the U.S. Declaration of Independence; in fact, Jefferson, then in Paris as American minister, advised on its drafting. It remains part of France's constitutional law.

events.title: Haitian Revolution Begins
events.blurb: A voodoo ceremony in a wooded area of a French Caribbean sugar colony marked the coordinated signal for a mass uprising of enslaved Africans. Within ten days, plantations across the northern plain were in flames and 4,000 whites and mulattos were dead. It was the largest slave revolt in the history of the Americas and the only one that successfully established an independent state. The colony had been the richest in the Western hemisphere; it produced 40 percent of the world's sugar.
events.revealBlurb: August 22, 1791 — Saint-Domingue (now Haiti). The ceremony was at Bois Caïman, led by voodoo priest Dutty Boukman. Toussaint Louverture emerged as principal leader, though he was captured by the French in 1802 and died in a freezing French prison cell. Independence came on January 1, 1804.

events.title: Napoleon Invades Russia
events.blurb: A French emperor crossed the Neman River into Russian territory with the largest army Europe had ever seen — 680,000 men drawn from across his continental empire. His objectives were to compel Russia back into a trade embargo against Britain and to break Russian military power. The Russians fell back, burning as they withdrew, refusing pitched battle. The French reached Moscow in September to find it empty and soon burning. The retreat home through a catastrophic winter would destroy almost the entire army.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1812 — the Neman crossing. Of the 680,000 who crossed east, perhaps 40,000 returned. The retreat featured the famous crossing of the Berezina River, where improvised pontoon bridges collapsed under packed refugees; tens of thousands died in the icy water.

events.title: Battle of Waterloo
events.blurb: A French emperor's army of 73,000 men, attempting to defeat the main Anglo-Allied and Prussian armies separately before they could unite, fought the Anglo-Allied force on a Belgian ridge for most of a muddy Sunday. The Prussian army arrived in the late afternoon on the emperor's right flank; by nightfall the French line had collapsed. The emperor fled; he surrendered to the British at a port three weeks later and was exiled to a rocky island in the South Atlantic.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1815 — Napoleon Bonaparte vs. the Duke of Wellington and Gebhard von Blücher. Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena and died there May 5, 1821. "Meet your Waterloo" — a decisive and final defeat — entered English as a phrase.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Erasmus Publishes Praise of Folly
events.blurb: A 44-year-old Dutch humanist scholar, passing a week at the London home of his friend Thomas More, dashed off a satirical essay in Latin in which a personified Folly delivered a self-congratulatory oration cataloguing the foolishnesses of every social station — pedantic scholars, superstitious monks, greedy merchants, bloody princes. The essay circulated across Europe in pirated editions within months; it would be read as a scathing critique of the corrupt Catholic Church.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Desiderius Erasmus. The pun of the title is trilingual: "Moriae Encomium" in Latin, pointing at Thomas More (Morus) as well as at folly. It was placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. More, who thought the essay funny, was canonized after being beheaded by Henry VIII.

events.title: Globe Theatre Opens
events.blurb: A London acting company, evicted from their original playhouse when their landlord refused to renew the lease, dismantled the building overnight, carried the timbers across the frozen Thames, and rebuilt them into a new circular theatre on the south bank. Their principal playwright and shareholder produced several of his greatest plays on its stage over the next 14 years, until a cannon effect during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.
events.revealBlurb: 1599 — the Lord Chamberlain's Men; William Shakespeare was a shareholder. It burned on June 29, 1613; was rebuilt; was demolished in 1644 under Puritan hostility to theatre. A faithful replica opened in 1997 near the original site.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Casablanca Premieres
events.blurb: A wartime romance set in a Moroccan cafe — produced on a tight schedule with an often-improvised script — premiered at a New York theater two weeks after Allied troops actually landed in the real-life city, a coincidence that boosted interest. The film's lead actor and actress had expected it to be a forgettable assignment; its dialogue's half-dozen phrases would be quoted by a century of audiences. Neither of the two stars was anyone's first choice for their parts.
events.revealBlurb: November 26, 1942 — Hollywood Theatre, NYC. Director Michael Curtiz, stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman. "Here's looking at you, kid" was Bogart's improvisation. "Play it again, Sam" is never actually said in the film.

events.title: The Seventh Seal Released
events.blurb: A Swedish director released a 96-minute black-and-white film about a disillusioned medieval knight, returning from the Crusades to find his homeland ravaged by plague, who plays an extended chess match with a personification of Death to postpone his own. The film's signature image — the knight and Death on a beach chessboard — entered the pantheon of instantly recognizable cinema shots, as did its bleak allegorical mode.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 1957 — Ingmar Bergman, with Max von Sydow as the knight. The chess game has been parodied by Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey, the Muppets, and South Park, among dozens of others. Bergman wrote the screenplay in two weeks.

events.title: Jaws Released
events.blurb: A 28-year-old director released a 124-minute thriller about a great white shark terrorizing a New England beach resort. Principal photography, supposed to last 55 days, ran 159; the mechanical shark broke down constantly and was rarely shown, producing the film's signature off-screen menace. Released across a record number of screens nationwide with a saturation TV ad campaign, it invented the summer blockbuster.
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1975 — Steven Spielberg. The shark's malfunctions forced Spielberg to rely on John Williams' two-note score to telegraph the threat. The film caused a measurable drop in US beach attendance for years afterward.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Stonehenge Completed
events.blurb: Over the course of a millennium, Neolithic builders on a chalk plain in southern England erected a circular arrangement of massive standing stones — some weighing 25 tonnes, dragged from quarries over 250 kilometres away — fitted together with mortise-and-tenon joints as if they were timber. The monument aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Its precise purpose — ritual, astronomical, funerary — has been debated for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2000 BCE — main sarsen-circle completion on Salisbury Plain. The smaller "bluestones," of volcanic rock, came from the Preseli Hills in Wales. Construction had begun about 5,000 years ago in earthen-bank form. The monument predates the druids by 2,000 years, despite the misattribution.

events.title: Taj Mahal Completed
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor completed, 22 years after his beloved queen's death in childbirth, a white-marble mausoleum for her on the bank of a river in a North Indian city. Some 20,000 craftsmen worked on the main structure alone; the dome rises 73 metres, inlaid with semiprecious stones in floral and calligraphic patterns. A matching mosque flanks one side of the tomb; a guest house mirrors it on the other. The emperor's own body joined hers in the crypt in 1666.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1648 — Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. The architectural team was led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori. An apocryphal legend claims Shah Jahan cut off the master builders' hands; there is no historical evidence for it. The monument changes colour subtly throughout the day.

events.title: Versailles Hall of Mirrors Completed
events.blurb: A French king's chief architect and royal painter completed the centerpiece of a vastly enlarged royal palace on the edge of Paris — a 73-metre-long gallery of 578 mirror panels on one side, facing 17 tall windows overlooking the palace gardens on the other, with a vaulted ceiling painted with 30 scenes of the king's military triumphs. Mirrors were at the time so expensive that a single pane could cost as much as a small estate; the gallery was a showcase of French glassmaking independence from Venice.
events.revealBlurb: 1684 — Jules Hardouin-Mansart (architect) and Charles Le Brun (painter) for Louis XIV. The Treaty of Versailles ending WWI was signed in the room on June 28, 1919 — a deliberate German humiliation in the same space where German unification had been proclaimed in 1871.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Panama Canal Opens
events.blurb: A 77-kilometre canal cutting across the narrowest part of the Central American isthmus opened to international shipping, after a US-run construction effort that had finished a French attempt abandoned two decades earlier amid malaria, yellow fever, and bankruptcy. The canal used a system of locks to raise ships 26 metres above sea level across the continental divide. It cut the sea route from New York to San Francisco by over 12,000 kilometres.
