events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1914 — the ship SS Ancon made the first full transit. The American construction was made possible partly by controlling yellow fever and malaria through mosquito eradication. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties returned the canal to Panamanian sovereignty in 1999.

events.title: Fall of France
events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.

events.title: Atlantic Charter
events.blurb: The leader of a neutral superpower and the leader of a beleaguered island nation met secretly aboard warships anchored off a foggy Newfoundland coast and jointly published a declaration of eight principles for the postwar world — including self-determination for peoples, freedom of the seas, and disarmament of aggressor nations — without committing either country to fight.
events.revealBlurb: August 14, 1941 — FDR and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter from HMS Prince of Wales and USS Augusta in Placentia Bay. The US was still technically neutral. The document became the founding framework for the United Nations. Churchill later noted that when the two men sang "O God Our Help in Ages Past" on deck, he felt the war was won.

events.title: Operation Barbarossa
events.blurb: Three million soldiers, 600,000 motorised vehicles, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft crossed a 2,900-kilometre border in the pre-dawn darkness, launching the largest land invasion in military history. The defender's air force lost over a thousand planes in the first day, many of them still on the ground.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1941. Stalin reportedly refused to believe his own border commanders' early reports and assumed the attacks were unauthorised provocations. The operation's codename referenced the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. By December, Germany had advanced 1,000 km but failed to knock the Soviet Union out of the war.

events.title: Italy's Armistice Announcement
events.blurb: A radio broadcast by a head of government announced that his country had signed an armistice with the opposing alliance, pulling out of an axis it had helped found, leaving its former partner's forces — which had already occupied key positions across the country — to decide how to respond. German forces immediately disarmed Italian troops and occupied cities across the peninsula.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1943 — Marshal Badoglio's broadcast at 7:42 PM. The armistice had actually been signed on September 3 but was kept secret. German Operation Achse activated within hours, disarming and capturing roughly 650,000 Italian soldiers. Many were sent to German labour camps; some 50,000 died in captivity. The king and Badoglio fled Rome before dawn.

events.title: Death of Franklin Roosevelt
events.blurb: A president who had led his country through twelve years of depression and global conflict collapsed while sitting for a portrait at a cottage in the hills, dying two hours later before anyone could reach him, leaving a vice president who had been kept so far from the centre of power that he did not even know his government had been secretly building an atomic bomb.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1945 — FDR died at 3:35 PM at the Little White House in Warm Springs, Georgia. Harry Truman was presiding over the Senate when a note summoned him to the White House. His first question to Eleanor Roosevelt was whether he could do anything for her; she replied: "Is there anything we can do for you? For you are the one in trouble now."

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Released for Sega Genesis
events.blurb: Sega needed a mascot to fight Mario. The result was a blue hedgehog who could run faster than the screen could scroll, built around a physics engine that turned speed itself into the core gameplay mechanic. It shipped bundled with the Genesis in North America, helped Sega capture 65 percent of the console market.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1991 — Sonic the Hedgehog launched in North America for the Sega Genesis. Sega's North American market share climbed from 15% to 65% during the game's first year. The Sonic franchise has since sold over 1.5 billion games.

events.title: Doom Uploaded to the Internet
events.blurb: At midnight, id Software attempted to upload its new game to a university FTP server. So many people were already waiting that the network collapsed. When the file finally went live, 10,000 simultaneous downloads crashed it again. Doom popularised the first-person shooter genre, the shareware distribution model, online multiplayer, user-generated mods, and the moral panic about video game violence — all within a few months.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1993 — id Software uploaded Doom to an FTP server at the University of Wisconsin–Madison after working 30 consecutive hours. The game sold over 2 million retail copies and was installed on an estimated 10 million PCs via shareware by 1995.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Berlin Airlift Begins
events.blurb: When Soviet forces blockaded all land and water routes into the western sectors of a divided city, Western powers responded with the largest humanitarian airlift in history. At peak, a transport plane landed every 30 seconds, carrying 8,000 tons of coal, flour, and medicine a day to 2.5 million stranded residents.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1948 — the blockade began; the airlift launched two days later and ran 15 months. Pilots dropped candy bars on tiny parachutes for watching children; one became known as the "Candy Bomber." 101 people died during the operation.

events.title: Korean War Begins
events.blurb: In the pre-dawn darkness, roughly 75,000 soldiers of a northern peninsular state poured south across the 38th parallel, overwhelming border defenses and driving south within days. The United Nations Security Council, with the Soviet representative boycotting, voted to intervene — the first shooting war between major powers since 1945.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1950 — Kim Il-sung's forces crossed the parallel. The USSR was boycotting the UN over China's representation, which is why the Soviet veto didn't stop intervention. MacArthur's Inchon landing three months later turned the war.

events.title: SDI Announced
events.blurb: In a televised address from the Oval Office, a U.S. president proposed a space-based missile defense shield intended to render nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete." Critics dubbed it "Star Wars" and scientists called it technically unachievable. Whatever its technical merits, the announcement terrified the Kremlin and forced Soviet planners to contemplate a ruinous new arms race they could not afford.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1983 — Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative. It never produced a working system, but it contributed to Soviet economic exhaustion. Some historians credit SDI with accelerating Gorbachev's arms-control pivot by years.

events.title: August Coup Against Gorbachev
events.blurb: A committee of Soviet hardliners — the KGB chief, the defense minister, the vice president — placed the reform-minded Soviet leader under house arrest at his Black Sea dacha and announced on state television that he was "unwell." Three days of confusion followed. A reformist Russian president climbed atop a tank outside his parliament and defied the plotters. The coup collapsed in 60 hours, and so, effectively, did the union.
events.revealBlurb: August 19-21, 1991 — the tank-top defier was Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find his authority gutted; Yeltsin had eclipsed him. Within four months the USSR itself would be gone.

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: Epic of Gilgamesh Compiled
events.blurb: Mesopotamian scribes compiled the standard version of a long cuneiform poem about a semi-legendary king of a Sumerian city, his wild-man companion, and a flood survivor they visit in search of immortality. Earlier Sumerian poems about the hero had been circulating for centuries; a single scribe, working in Akkadian, produced the integrated twelve-tablet version that survives. It is the oldest recognized work of narrative literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — standard Babylonian version attributed to the scribe Sin-liqe-unninni. The poem's flood narrative preceded the one in Genesis by at least 500 years. Rediscovered in fragments in 19th-century excavations of Nineveh.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: Anne Frank's Diary Published
events.blurb: Two years after the liberation of Nazi concentration camps and the death of his teenage daughter in one of them, a Dutch businessman published, after several rejections, an edited version of the diary she had kept during the two years her family had spent hiding in a secret annex behind his Amsterdam office. The book was a modest Dutch bestseller; translated into over 70 languages, it became the most widely read personal account of the Holocaust.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1947 — Otto Frank published "Het Achterhuis" ("The Secret Annex"). Anne had died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen in February 1945, two months before liberation. The diary has sold over 30 million copies.

events.title: Things Fall Apart Published
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Nigerian broadcaster published a short novel tracing the life of an Igbo wrestler and farmer in a southeastern Nigerian village and the arrival of English colonial missionaries that destroys his world. Written in English deliberately infused with Igbo idiom, the book pushed back against European literary stereotypes of African societies. It has since been translated into 50 languages and sold over 20 million copies — the most widely read book by any African author.
events.revealBlurb: 1958 — Chinua Achebe. Its title is from Yeats's poem "The Second Coming." Achebe later famously accused Joseph Conrad of racism in "Heart of Darkness." He was in a serious car crash in 1990 that left him paralyzed from the waist down; he continued writing for over two more decades.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Watson Wins Jeopardy
events.blurb: An IBM supercomputer named after the company's founder competed over three nights of a televised American trivia game show against the two greatest human champions the show had ever produced — and won by a wide margin. The machine had been fed a corpus of Wikipedia, encyclopedias, and dictionaries; it processed buzzer-triggered natural-language clues with a complex pipeline of heuristics and statistical models. It was not a single breakthrough; it was an engineering triumph.
events.revealBlurb: February 14-16, 2011 — Watson vs. Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. Jennings' final written answer on night three: "I, for one, welcome our new computer overlords." IBM spent heavily trying to commercialize Watson for healthcare and business; most of those products have since been divested or discontinued.

events.title: Tesla Model S Released
events.blurb: A California electric-vehicle startup, founded a decade earlier and funded partly by the same entrepreneur who had sold PayPal, delivered the first units of a four-door luxury sedan with a fully electric drivetrain, over-the-air software updates, a 17-inch touchscreen, and a 500-kilometre range. Legacy automakers had considered electric cars a niche; the Model S made them convincingly better than gasoline vehicles in several important dimensions.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 2012 — Tesla Model S, led by Elon Musk. Motor Trend named it Car of the Year. The "Ludicrous Mode" software option made it accelerate 0-60 mph in under 3 seconds. Tesla passed $1 trillion valuation in 2021, briefly the first automaker to do so.

events.title: Pelé Wins First World Cup
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Brazilian forward, playing in his first senior international tournament, scored two goals in the World Cup final as Brazil beat the host nation 5-2 to win football's greatest prize for the first time in the country's history. He became the youngest player ever to score in a World Cup final; his performance vaulted Brazilian football onto the world stage. He would go on to win two more World Cups over the following 12 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 29, 1958 — Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento) at the Råsunda Stadium, Solna, Sweden. Brazil 5, Sweden 2. Pelé was carried off the field by his teammates at the end. He remains the only player to win three World Cups.

events.title: Wilt Chamberlain's 100-Point Game
events.blurb: A 25-year-old 7-foot-1 Philadelphia Warriors center scored 100 points in a regular-season NBA game — 36 field goals, 28 free throws, a record that has never been approached since. The game, played at a neutral-site arena in a central Pennsylvania city, drew only 4,124 spectators; no television footage survives, and only one photograph of the 100-point moment exists. The center himself had scored 50 on a different occasion just weeks earlier; a 100-point game almost seemed inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1962 — Wilt Chamberlain, Philadelphia vs. New York Knicks at Hershey, PA. Final score: Warriors 169, Knicks 147. The iconic photo shows Chamberlain holding a piece of paper reading "100" in the locker room. His career scoring average of 30.1 points per game remains second only to Michael Jordan.

events.title: Munich Olympics Massacre
events.blurb: Eight armed members of a Palestinian militant group scaled the perimeter fence of an Olympic Village at a German Summer Games, broke into the Israeli team's dormitory apartments, killed two Israeli athletes on the spot, and took nine others hostage. An inept German rescue operation at the military airfield where the hostages and captors had been flown ended with all nine hostages dead along with five of the eight attackers and one German police officer. The Games were suspended for a day, then resumed; the IOC president said that "the Games must go on."
events.revealBlurb: September 5-6, 1972 — Black September. IOC president: Avery Brundage. Israel's government launched a covert years-long assassination campaign against the attack's planners, known as Operation Wrath of God and dramatized in Spielberg's Munich (2005).

events.title: Maradona's Hand of God & Goal of the Century
events.blurb: An Argentine forward, playing a World Cup quarterfinal against England four years after a war over Atlantic islands the two countries had fought, scored two goals in four minutes. The first was a blatant handball that the referee missed; the player later described it as scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God." The second, four minutes later, was a solo 60-metre dribble past five English players from the halfway line — widely considered the greatest goal in World Cup history.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1986 — Diego Maradona at Estadio Azteca, Mexico City. Argentina 2, England 1. Argentina went on to win the tournament. Maradona later admitted the first goal was not only illegal but intended as a kind of revenge for the Falklands War. He died at 60 in 2020; Argentina went into three days of national mourning.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964 Signed
events.blurb: President Lyndon Johnson signed the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations — ending the legal architecture of Jim Crow segregation. The bill passed after the longest Senate filibuster in history: 57 days.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1964 — The White House. Johnson reportedly told an aide after signing the bill, "We have lost the South for a generation" — a reference to the political realignment he expected. Johnson signed the bill with 75 ceremonial pens, handing them to civil rights leaders and the bill's sponsors.

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: Stonewall Riots
events.blurb: A routine police raid on a Mafia-owned gay bar in a Greenwich Village of Manhattan turned into a six-night uprising when patrons — many of them drag queens, street kids, and trans people of color — fought back rather than submit to arrest. The confrontation catalyzed the modern LGBTQ rights movement; the first Pride marches were held on its first anniversary.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 1969 — Stonewall Inn, NYC. Pivotal figures included Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera. The riot ignited the Gay Liberation Front, which modeled itself on the Black Panthers. June is now Pride Month across much of the world.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Hotmail Launched
events.blurb: Two engineers launched the world's first free web-based email service, deliberately choosing the launch date to coincide with a major American holiday celebrating independence. Users for the first time could access their email from any computer with a browser, independent of any particular ISP or employer. The service picked up a million users in six months.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1996 — Sabeer Bhatia and Jack Smith. They chose Independence Day to symbolize freedom from ISP lock-in. Microsoft acquired the service for $400 million 18 months later; it evolved into Outlook.com.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Reddit Founded
events.blurb: Two 22-year-old University of Virginia roommates who had just moved to Massachusetts on a Y Combinator fellowship launched a link-aggregation and discussion site that would, over the next two decades, become what its users called "the front page of the internet." The initial userbase was boosted by the founders themselves maintaining dozens of fake accounts to seed discussions. They sold the site to Condé Nast 16 months later for a reported $10-20 million.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 2005 — Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian; later joined by Aaron Swartz, the open-internet activist who would die in 2013 facing federal prosecution. The site's iconic mascot, Snoo, was designed by Ohanian on a napkin.

events.title: Pokémon Go Released
events.blurb: A free mobile game combining augmented reality with a beloved monster-catching franchise launched initially in Australia, New Zealand, and the United States. Within a week, 21 million daily active users were wandering streets and parks staring at their phones, discovering virtual creatures superimposed on physical landmarks. It became the fastest mobile game to reach $500 million in revenue and, more strikingly, got millions of sedentary users to walk outside.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Niantic Inc. Within weeks, fatal accidents, trespassing incidents, and a small bump in physical activity had all been documented. The Pokémon Go wedding, held in New York's Central Park, was among the odder cultural moments of mid-2016.

events.title: Tunguska Event
events.blurb: A massive explosion in the atmosphere above a remote Siberian forest flattened some 80 million trees over an area of 2,150 square kilometres. Eyewitnesses 60 kilometres away were thrown from their chairs. Seismic stations across Europe registered the blast. The first scientific expedition did not reach the site for 19 years. No impact crater was ever found.
events.revealBlurb: June 30, 1908 — Tunguska, Russian Empire. Current consensus: a stony asteroid 50-60 metres across exploded about 8 kilometres up. If it had arrived five hours later, it would have hit St. Petersburg. The date is now International Asteroid Day.

events.title: 1931 China Floods
events.blurb: A succession of heavy snowmelt and monsoon rains caused the three great rivers of central China to breach their banks simultaneously, flooding 180,000 square kilometres of farmland and cities. Estimates of the death toll range from 500,000 to 4 million; much of the toll came from subsequent famine and water-borne disease. It is likely the deadliest non-pandemic natural disaster in recorded history.
events.revealBlurb: July-November 1931 — Yangtze, Yellow, and Huai rivers. Wuhan was submerged for months. A young Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government was blamed for the weak response; flood relief was a major propaganda opportunity for the Communists in Jiangxi.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: Turkey-Syria Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck in the pre-dawn darkness along the fault separating the Anatolian and Arabian tectonic plates, followed nine hours later by a nearly equal-magnitude aftershock. Over 59,000 people died across southern Turkey and northern Syria; 1.5 million were left homeless. Shoddy building construction, exempted from code over years of amnesty laws, drew furious public blame.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 2023 — epicenter near Gaziantep. The disaster reshaped the Turkish elections three months later; contractors who had benefited from construction amnesties were prosecuted. In Syria, ongoing civil war hampered aid delivery.
